subtype: Approach: reviews and updates the checklist after each incident [Revision]
passage: Chetan here, writing what I saw in our release review on Friday. The release to the client had gone out without the config file for their test server, so they could not log in for two hours. Nobody was blamed. Sarita, who leads us, opened the release checklist on the shared screen and asked one thing: "Which line would have caught this?" There was none, so we added one: client config file attached and opened. Then Sarita scrolled and pointed at two lines, one for a tool we retired in March and one for a manual copy that the pipeline does now. We deleted both. The list went from fourteen lines to thirteen. I cannot tell how everyone felt, but the room was calmer, and people said the shorter list was easier to actually read.

qa.q: How many lines did the list have afterwards?
qa.a: The list went from fourteen lines to thirteen.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt going into the review meeting?
qa.a: Sarita seemed calm and determined, wanting the team to learn from the missed step without blaming anyone.

qa.q: What else could the team do to keep the list from going stale?
qa.a: The team could go through the list at regular times, not only after a problem, and ask which lines still matter.

qa.q: How might the client have been affected by the release?
qa.a: The client could not log in for two hours, so was probably frustrated and held up until the file was sorted out.

grounding: Shows a team adding one checklist line after a missed release step and deleting two outdated ones.
